multipleChoice.question: Which statement best captures the pattern introduced at the beginning of the discussion?
options: Couples generally divide domestic work according to their paid working hours.
Time-consuming chores are mainly a problem in places without modern equipment.
Women often carry a larger share of household and unpaid care work.
Men contribute less at home because they usually work in agriculture.

multipleChoice.question: According to the UN Women figures, how much more time do women spend on unpaid care and domestic work each day?
options: About three hours
About one hour
About two hours
About four hours

multipleChoice.question: Which pair of activities traditionally belongs to men's work on Rote?
options: Caring for children and older people
Cooking meals and sweeping floors
Washing dishes and cleaning homes
Growing rice and catching fish

multipleChoice.question: Why do domestic chores take so long on Rote?
options: Homes are far from the farming and fishing areas.
Washing machines are scarce and running water is unavailable.
Women must attend community workshops before starting chores.
Community leaders require all household work to be done by hand.

multipleChoice.question: Why is the apparently fair division of labour on Rote misleading?
options: Men are responsible for most care work as well as farming.
Women replace their household duties with work in the fields.
Women add farming or fishing work to their domestic responsibilities.
Men and women exchange their roles at different times each day.

multipleChoice.question: How is the expression "women's work" presented in the discussion of Rote?
options: As a negative label for repetitive chores traditionally assigned by gender
As a neutral name for the paid occupations available to island women
As a respectful title for women who manage community projects
As a temporary description of duties performed while men are in the fields

multipleChoice.question: What view supports the design of the Superdads workshops in Croatia?
options: Mothers should leave their careers so that they can rest more.
Only adult men, rather than boys, need to change their domestic habits.
Wealthy countries have already achieved an equal sharing of care work.
Fathers and sons can ease mothers' burden by sharing household tasks.

multipleChoice.question: What can be inferred from the benefits described for mothers when men share the chores?
options: Domestic work affects only mothers who are pursuing careers.
An unequal workload can limit mothers' time for personal goals and rest.
Mothers usually value hobbies more than help from family members.
Men's participation removes every source of conflict within the home.

multipleChoice.question: Why are careers, hobbies and rest listed in the discussion?
options: To illustrate different ways mothers could use time freed by shared chores
To rank the three activities that mothers value most highly
To show that paid employment is the only meaningful form of relief
To explain why mothers become less willing to complete household duties

multipleChoice.question: What overall implication is shared by the two NGO projects?
options: Unequal housework can be solved only in remote communities.
Better equipment is more important than changing family attitudes.
Fairer sharing of housework can improve the wellbeing of the household.
Every family member must perform exactly the same domestic tasks.
